question: How do off-policy and trust-region policy gradient algorithms (Off-PAC, DPG, DDPG, TD3, TRPO, PPO and others) work, and which should a practitioner use?
contributions: Explains importance sampling and off-policy learning
Walks through GTD, Off-PAC, DPG, DDPG, TD3, NPG/TRPO, PPO, Retrace, ACER, ACKTR, emphatic methods
Case study: DDPG recommender (Wang et al.)
Worked example: PPO on a real and simulated servo motor

limits: No benchmark data of the author's own beyond a one-servo toy task; no seeds, no error bars, no network sizes given for the servo experiment.
Equations are images; the chapter's algorithm boxes were not recoverable as text.
Wang et al. recommender tested only in simulation (author notes this).
Dated for LLM work: covers 2020-era continuous control; the author states TRPO/DDPG-type methods and offers no LLM RL guidance.
Author's own explanations (why CDQ helps Ant, why TPS helps) are labelled speculation ('I propose', 'I speculate').
practices: Use importance sampling to correct off-policy experience (Importance Sampling).
Prefer TD3 over DDPG (Which Algorithm Should I Use?).
Prefer a trust region method where a slight policy move can be disastrous (same section).
Always verify an implementation against the original paper and with monitoring code, unrolling loops by hand (TD3 tip).
Solve the next simplest problem first when debugging RL (servo tip).
Tune hyperparameters in a simulator before real hardware (servo section).
Use several episodes per update to de-correlate samples; smaller minibatches; tune value and policy networks independently; lower learning rate for stability (tuning tips).
Do not expect same result across framework DDPG implementations (DDPG implementation).
Avoid asynchronous methods unless wall-clock speed justifies the operational cost (Note on Asynchronous Methods).

specify a region in parameter space where gradient steps can be trusted, adjusting step size dynamically
